The per-entry loop skips an entry only when OpenSSL's first non-provider error is ERR_R_PASSED_INVALID_ARGUMENT. That covers unsupported suites and mandatory extensions, but OpenSSL's public_name checks in ech_final_config_checks() fail without raising that code, so those entries are treated as malformed input and the whole list is rejected:

```python
good = ECH_CONFIG[2:]
bad = bytearray(good)
i = bad.index(b'localhost'); bad[i + 8] = ord('.')   # "localhos." (trailing dot)
entries = good + bytes(bad)
ctx.set_ech_config(len(entries).to_bytes(2, 'big') + entries)
# ssl.SSLError: [SSL] internal error
```

[RFC 9849 6.1.7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9849/#name-authenticating-for-the-publ) says clients SHOULD ignore an ECHConfig whose public_name isn't a valid host name, so I'd expect the good entry to be used here. It is only a SHOULD, so I'm not suggesting this blocks the PR.

My bigger worry is that skip-versus-fail depends on which internal OpenSSL path happens to raise which error code, and that can change between OpenSSL releases without anyone noticing. Two thoughts:

- Could we ask OpenSSL to provide a way to load a list while skipping unusable entries, and treat this loop as a stopgap with a comment saying so? I guess OpenSSL 4.0.x has shipped so that API surface is presumably already set in stone...
- Whatever we keep, a test with one unusable entry of each kind (unsupported suite, mandatory extension, bad public_name) next to a good one would pin the behavior. test_mixed_ech_config_versions only covers the unknown-version case.
I removed this code, so this is moot.

When the two-byte length prefix doesn't match, the buffer goes to OSSL_ECHSTORE_read_echconfiglist() as-is, and that function auto-detects base64. So this succeeds:

```python
ctx.set_ech_config(base64.b64encode(ECH_CONFIG))
```

The docs say the argument is "a binary-encoded ECHConfigList". Was accepting base64 intended? If so, it should be documented and tested. If not, I'd reject anything that fails the length-prefix check here, which also means every accepted input goes through the per-entry loop above and gets the same skip-unusable-entries behaviour. Right now a base64 list takes OpenSSL's all-or-nothing path instead.

I decided to just remove the length-prefix validation. That means we're technically not compliant with the RFC, but the code to check this is complicated, and we should merely expose OpenSSL's behavior rather than inventing our own.

As such, I documented the support for base64, since that's what OpenSSL also supports.

SSLSocket.set_ech_config() and the ech_config= argument reject server-side use, but the context methods don't check the role at all. Both of these succeed silently:

```python
ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER).set_ech_config(config)
ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT).load_ech_keys("ech.pem")
```

For PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT and PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER contexts the role is known, so raising would be consistent with the socket level and with how newPySSLSocket() rejects mismatched roles. PROTOCOL_TLS contexts would have to stay permissive.

This is added and test_set_outer_server_name exercises it through _sslobj, but there is no wrapper in ssl.py and no documentation, so users can't reach it. Is it meant to be public in this PR?

If so, it needs the wrapper and docs, and I'd expect the same guards as set_ech_config(): client side only, and only before the handshake starts.

If we don't want to do that, leave it out?
Removed it. This was in the original DEfO PR, but I think they forgot about it.

Instead of storing the raw distrusted certiificates and memcmp comparing them, lets not trigger binary scanners looking for the key strings and store sha256 of the distrusted .der values and compare spki to .der via sha256 hash.  I think Go did the same thing. (and is how Chrome CRLSet works?)

Yes, Golang uses the SHA2-256 digest of the SPKI. My first implementation used the same approach. I rewrote it to use the raw SPKI because it was less complicated in C and probably a tiny bit faster, too. It didn't occur to me that some scanners could look for SPKI DER in binaries ... fair point.

Back to the drawing board!
Latest commit now uses SHA2-256 SPKI fingerprint. Contrary to Golang I'm using binary notation for the fingerprint. It feels to silly to convert bytes to hexdigest and then `strncmp()`.

Maybe use `SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH` instead of `sizeof(_distrusted_spki[i])`. If the array changes to become an array of `char*`, sizeof() would be wrong.

```suggestion
        if (memcmp(digest, _distrusted_spki[i], SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH) == 0) {
```
Why would anybody want to change the type of the struct? And wouldn't your example result in an out-of-bounds read?

> Why would anybody want to change the type of the struct

If we could predict something like that, we'd have made the type correct in the first place. Since we know we can't predict, we try and make a habit of coding defensively in places where we can predict a second-order effect. The most likely reason I can see for it changing is to accommodate compiler type weirdness (which is something Victor deals with a lot, so I'm not surprised he makes the suggestion).

If the type _did_ change, the `sizeof` could go from comparing all bits to only the first 8, which would be a catastrophic loss of entropy 😉 

(No comment on whether the proposed constant is connect, but an out-of-bounds read is easier to detect at runtime than a short read, and there are definitely ways to have the pointer reference the right amount of memory without `sizeof` being able to calculate it.)
If somebody mess up the struct and change the data structure to `char *`, then `digest_len != sizeof(_distrusted_spki[0])` triggers, the function returns `-1` and every handshake fails.

Can we use `digest_len` as the comparison then? Or something else that is known good but doesn't depend on the compiler? That's the concern that is motivating Victor's request here - `sizeof` of a dereferenced pointer type is about as unpredictable as it gets.

If it makes you and Victor happy and gets this PR landed... okay. I don't think it's necessary, though.

The latest commit now asserts() the size of array members and compares against `SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH`
